The Public Record Behind the November 3, 2026 Ballot
Chesterfield County, South Carolina

This page does not tell anyone how to vote. Eight incumbents on this ballot have no opponent. Each has a panel below, built the way an institution introduces its own board members — the office, the officeholder, what they did, whom they are connected to, and what the record does not show — but filled from the public record rather than a press release: biographies, bill records, sponsor lists, election returns, minutes, Attorney General opinions and court records. The office

The House's page for the seat today: District 54 - Chesterfield, Darlington, Dillon & Marlboro Counties. Representatives are considered part-time citizen legislators who serve two-year terms. luck_scstatehouse_member.txtluck_wikipedia_sc_house.txt

A thirteen-slide post on his page: all appropriations, whether Democratic or Republican, House or Senate, have been removed from the FY2026-2027 budget. The money for the Lake Paul Wallace dam is IN the budget. 01_luck_budget_slide01_appropriations.txt02_luck_budget_slide02_lake_paul_wallace.txt

What the public record does not show

None of his seventeen prime-sponsored entries, and neither of the two news reports of his re-election filing, mentions the county detention center, a jail, the referendum, a State Law Enforcement Division inquiry, the school district's audit, or McBee. luck_sponsor_search_126.txtluck_wpde_2026_reelection.txtluck_heraldadvocate_2026_reelection.txtsearched: the file tagged; terms: detention · jail · referendum · SLED · audit · McBee

Luck has not publicly addressed the detention center deaths, the SLED investigation, or the governance structure documented on this page. His district includes the communities where these events occurred. His silence is not unusual for a first-term legislator. It is noted because the question of who represents the people of Chesterfield County in the General Assembly is the question this page asks — and the answer, for District Fifty-Four, is a freshman member who has not yet used the position to address the documented failures in the county he represents.

Chesterfield County Probate Judge · Democratic

Gail Blizzard Ingram

Judge Ingram began her service as Chesterfield County Probate Judge on January 5, 2015.

›

The office

The statute: There is established in each of the counties of this State a probate court, which must be located at the county seat … The probate court of each county is part of the unified judicial system of this State. HISTORY: 1976 Act No. 690. ingram_t14c023.txt

The court system's description: Each county has a Probate Judge who is popularly elected to a four-year term and has jurisdiction over marriage licenses, estates of deceased persons, guardianships of incompetents, conservatorships of estates of minors and incompetents, minor settlements under $25,000 and involuntary commitments to institutions for mentally ill and/or chemically dependent persons. They also have exclusive jurisdiction over trusts. ingram_probate_court.txt

Who may hold it: No person is eligible to hold the office of judge of probate who is not at the time of his election a citizen of the United States and of this State, has not attained the age of twenty-one years upon his election, has not become a qualified elector of the county in which he is to be a judge, and has not received a four-year bachelor's degree from an accredited post-secondary institution or if he has received no degree he must have four years' experience as an employee in a probate judge's office in this State. The Code's own note on that last condition: has not been precleared by the U.S. Department of Justice and cannot be put into effect. No law degree is required. ingram_t14c023.txt

A vacancy: Vacancies for unexpired terms in the offices of judge of probate may be filled by the Governor with the advice and consent of the Senate. ingram_t14c023.txt

How Ingram filed with the State Election Commission: How they filed.

The officeholder

The court's biography: The Honorable Gail B. Ingram graduated as valedictorian of Lower Richland High School in 1975, going on to attend the University of South Carolina, graduating magna cum laude with a B. A. in history in 1978 and a M.A.T. in history in 1980. She studied as an exchange student at the Warwick University in Coventry, England from 1977-1978. ingram_bio.txt

During her 34-year career as a high school history teacher, she completed 30 hours above the master's level and earned the prestigious National Board Certification in social studies and history in 2004. The DAR named her as the Outstanding Teacher of American History for SC in 1997. She also serves as the Chesterfield County Drug Court Judge and the Veterans Treatment Court Judge for the 4th Judicial Circuit. ingram_bio.txt

The school, from the House's resolution of 2002: Gail B. Ingram, a teacher at Cheraw High School, received the Richard T. Farrell Teacher of Merit Award for being selected as the National History Day Teacher of the Year for 2001-2002. ingram_h5218_2002.txt

A travel company's profile of her: My twin sister and I were born in Tokyo, Japan, in 1956. including the Patricia Behring Teacher of the Year Award this year (the profile carries no date). ingram_ef_spotlight.txt

The seat's history

The holder before her

The Senate's resolution on his retirement: the Honorable Edwin "Brother" Malloy Davis will begin a well-deserved retirement after twenty-nine years as a highly-regarded probate court judge in Chesterfield County; then as the Chesterfield County Veterans' Affairs officer before becoming the county's probate judge; appointed by Governor Dick Riley as Chesterfield County probate judge on July 1, 1985, Judge Davis has served longer than any other probate judge in Chesterfield County since the Civil War. He did not seek re-election in 2014 but retired at the end of his final term. ingram_s368_2015.txt

Two holders of the office since the mid-nineteen-eighties: Davis, first appointed by the Governor, then Ingram. No list of earlier holders was found online.

Documented conduct

The drug court

The Solicitor's Office, June 23, 2025: Previously, Darlington County Drug Court was held virtually for participants with Chesterfield County Probate Judge Gail Ingram presiding. Chief Justice John Kittredge appointed Darlington County Magistrate Judge Craig La Cross as the Drug Court Judge for Darlington at Solicitor Burch's request. 14_drug_court_june2025_ingram_lacross_burch.txt

The treatment provider, sharing it: We are grateful to be a part of the drug court program! Thank you Fourth Circuit Solicitor's Office, Paul M. Burch, Jr. for making this happen! 14_drug_court_june2025_ingram_lacross_burch.txt

The first graduation, Monday, January 12, 2026: The ceremony was convened by Judge LaCross and included a formal call to order, a motion by the State presented by Solicitor Paul "Mike" Burch Jr. Guest speaker Judge Gail Ingram addressed the graduates; closing remarks from Solicitor Burch and Heather Clark of Rubicon, a key treatment and recovery partner in the program. 15_drug_court_graduation_jan2026.txt

By the Solicitor’s Office’s own account, the drug court judge was appointed at the Solicitor’s request; the probate judge presided over it before, and spoke at its first graduation.

Connection points

A law firm in her county, on its own page: Ingram Law Firm accepts Probate Court cases in Marlboro County and Darlington County. Ingram Law Firm accepts only uncontested probate matters in Chesterfield County. ingram_cherawlaw_probate_court.txt

The same firm's biography of its founding attorney: Miller is married to Gail B. Ingram, who taught high school in Cheraw for 34 years before retiring and being elected Chesterfield County Probate Judge. Miller retired from the practice of law in 2025, after 47 years of helping clients. Its attorneys page lists Mark K. Ingram Attorney, whose practice areas include Probate Court. ingram_cherawlaw_miller.txtingram_cherawlaw_attorneys.txt

The firm limits its Chesterfield County probate work to uncontested matters; the page states that limit and no other arrangement.

The surname in county government: After 26 years as Cheraw's mayor and more than 40 years in Chesterfield County governments, Andy Ingram chose not to run for reelection (Dec 30, 2023). Northeastern Technical College's chart dated August 2025 lists Program Manager I Andrew Ingram. pc_andy_ingram.txtnetc_org_chart_b1.txt

No record gathered for this page states how, or whether, Andy Ingram is related to the judge or to the law firm. The shared surname is all the record shows.

Her post of July 25, 2019: Andrew McLeod and Miller Ingram, Eagle Scouts and attorneys, received the 2019 Distinguished Citizen Award from the Pee Dee Area Council of the Boy Scouts of America this evening at a reception held at Northeastern Technical College. Mark Ingram, also an Eagle Scout and attorney, presented his father with the award. 16_ingram_family_bsa_award_2019.txt

One senator appears in two records on this page: he co-sponsored the Senate's resolution on her predecessor's retirement, Sponsors: Senators Sheheen and Malloy, and he is listed among the Senators voting for Paul M. Burch - 37 in the joint election for the circuit seat: Malloy, Gerald. ingram_s368_2015.txtElection to Circuit Court, 4th Jud, Seat _Joint Election Vote Number 19_.pdf

Ingram is not accused of misconduct. She is documented as occupying a position that has been held by two people across four decades, in a county where the probate attorney practices through a firm that limits its Chesterfield County work to uncontested matters in the same court, the drug court she presided over was convened at the request of the Fourth Circuit Solicitor, and the institution that hosted the reception where one of the firm's attorneys received a civic award is staffed by the school board's former officers. The question is not what Ingram has done wrong. The question is what happens to a probate matter, a drug court referral, or a civic recognition when every path through the system passes through the same network — and no one outside that network has held the seat long enough to remember what independence looks like.

His opponent in the special general, Jordan C. Seidhom (R), is a signer of the county's sales-tax commission resolution that set this year's referendum question: Jordan Seidhom - signed. council_bp_brand_2025.txtres_2026-02_signature_transcription.txt

Name: Temecha McColl Brand filed a Statement of Intent on Date Received: 8/14/26 to challenge Darin Coleman for Office: School board district 2. Coleman filed eleven days earlier, on Date Received: 8/3/2026. TbrandSOI2026.txtDcolemanSOI2026.txt

Coleman has held the District Two seat since two thousand ten — sixteen years. He is simultaneously employed as Dean of Student Engagement at Northeastern Technical College, where he supervises student life at the Pageland campus that serves the same community his board seat governs. Coleman has no campaign page, no campaign hashtag, and no documented campaign activity since filing. Temecka Brand has a full campaign infrastructure — a dedicated page, a biographical introduction, policy posts citing the district's own performance data, and community endorsements.

Both filed from the same address. If Temecka Brand wins, one household holds both County Council District Two and School Board District Two — the county budget authority and the school district policy authority for the same geographic district. The governance concentration is not a dual-office violation — two different people, two different bodies — but it places both the funding pipeline and the education oversight for one district under one roof. The interest that holds the chair does not change when the name changes.

Documented conduct

Her posts on the detention center

August 5, a post Facebook labels AI content: Our current detention center was built in 1972. Estimated Project Cost: $50 MILLION If it is not approved, the county anticipates funding the project through a property tax (millage) increase. 19_anderson_detention_center_aug5.txt

August 11: CMAR stands for Construction Manager at Risk. We have reached out to our delegations at both the state and federal levels without success. 21_anderson_detention_faq_aug11.txt

The dual-office record

QC News, May four, two thousand twenty-three: Barr confirmed that Councilwoman Mary Anderson held a seat on the Cheraw Board of Architectural Review simultaneously with her County Council seat from two thousand fourteen through December thirty-one, two thousand twenty-two. Anderson was appointed to the town board in two thousand fourteen, then won her council seat in November two thousand fourteen. She held both positions simultaneously for eight years. oct19_qcn_dualoffice_article_20230504.txt

QC News, May four, two thousand twenty-three, quoting Anderson: As we talked about Tuesday, during my appointed terms on the Board of Architectural Review, there was never an occasion where a conflict arose with my service as a County Council member. The simultaneous service never occurred to me to be a conflict. And: However, I now understand the issue with dual office holding and, had I been aware of that previously, I would have resigned my position on the Board. oct19_qcn_dualoffice_article_20230504.txt

QC News, May four, two thousand twenty-three, quoting Solicitor General Bob Cook's two thousand four Attorney General opinion: This Office has advised on at lease [sic] one prior occasion that a member of a local architectural review board holds an office for dual office holding purposes. And: The constitutional provisions prohibiting dual office holding would therefore be contravened. oct19_qcn_dualoffice_article_20230504.txt

Anderson held both positions for eight years. The town council awarded her for eight years of board service when she left the board. The AG opinion she was violating was published in two thousand four, ten years before she assumed the council seat. QC News also reported that state law governing architectural review boards states that none of the members may hold any other public office or position in the municipality or county. Anderson said she had no idea.

Project Hometown and the data pipeline

Project Hometown Cheraw is a relocation initiative funded by a three hundred five thousand dollar Southeast Crescent Regional Commission grant and administered through Main Street South Carolina and the Municipal Association of South Carolina. On September seventeenth, Anderson was published as its featured community profile. Ova Brown-Gillespie, of Chesterfield County Adult Education, was presented alongside Anderson in the same initiative. The civic function and the commercial enterprise are merged: the county council chair, the school district director, and the real estate broker-in-charge appear together in a nonprofit that attracts the residents and businesses Anderson's brokerage and council position both serve.

Lewis Realty and Whortleberry

Lewis Realty posted a listing for lots in Whortleberry, a newly established subdivision in Cheraw within town limits, with city water and sewer. The lots are priced at twenty-five thousand dollars for half an acre — adjacent to a FEMA Zone AE floodway along Huckleberry Branch. The listing does not reference the flood zone. The federal grant funds the recruitment program. The council chair lists the newly subdivided lots through her own brokerage in the community the recruitment program targets.

McLeod Health and the missing service

McLeod Health Cheraw announced that Labor and Delivery Care would no longer be offered, effective November first, two thousand eighteen. Anderson was on the McLeod Health Board of Trustees at the time — she was named as a trustee at the May two thousand eighteen Emergency Department ribbon cutting. The sixty million dollar replacement facility adds surgery, orthopedics, MRI, hospice beds, and a women's diagnostics center. It does not restore labor and delivery. A family recruited to Cheraw through Project Hometown cannot deliver a child at the hospital the council chair voted to build.

Two comments under the Project Hometown interview posed direct questions about the conflict between the council chair's McLeod board position and Lewis Realty's commercial position. Neither received a substantive response. The Project Hometown account replied with a link to its website.

The penny tax post

October twenty-second, two thousand twenty-four, Kim Burch posted: These are my views I am posting. oct17_kburch_pennytax_post_0758.txt

The board chair disclaims official capacity in the first sentence and exercises it in every sentence that follows. The same false binary — penny tax or property tax increase — appears in Mary Anderson's detention center FAQ, in Ethan Foard's WSOC interview, and in the county's own posts. "These are my views I am posting" refers to the views of the board chair, the former House member, the former economic development director, the former NETC commissioner. It does not refer to the views of a private person in the county.

The written statement to QC News

QC News, May four, two thousand twenty-three, printing Kimberly Burch's February eleven, two thousand twenty-three written statement: I am surprised that serving on an unpaid board that does not require an oath of office could possibly constitute dual office holding. And: I have conferred with an attorney who has expertise in governmental affairs and they took issue with the Attorney General's opinion regarding the issues at hand. They quickly pointed out that an Attorney General's opinion is only an opinion. There is no civil law precedent which addresses the questions you have raised. And: My attorney also opines that because of reasons stated above that the Courts would most likely rule that dual office only applies in cases where oaths of offices are required. And: One aspect of the law that is crystal clear is that I will continue to serve on the NETC board until a successor is appointed by the Delegation. oct19_qcn_dualoffice_article_20230504.txt

The Governor's letter

QC News, May four, two thousand twenty-three, quoting Governor Henry McMaster's Chief Legal Counsel Thomas Limehouse Jr., in a letter to the Chesterfield County Legislative Delegation dated February ten, two thousand twenty-three: Absent additional information or clarification, concurrent service by Ms. Burch on both the Commission and the School Board would seemingly violate the constitutional prohibition on dual-office holding. oct19_qcn_dualoffice_article_20230504.txt

QC News, May four, two thousand twenty-three, quoting the same Limehouse letter: However, because the Delegation has not recommended a successor, the Governor cannot make a new appointment. Consequently, the Office respectfully requests that the Delegation provide an update regarding the status of this seat (and the other Chesterfield County seat with an expired term) on the Commission. oct19_qcn_dualoffice_article_20230504.txt

QC News, Positions of Power video, February thirteen, two thousand twenty-three. Barr narration: The Governor also informed the delegation that eight of the nine Northeastern Technical College board members' terms are expired. The Governor asked the delegation to send him names so those members can be either reappointed or replaced. (auto-caption, corrected punctuation and proper nouns) oct19_qcn_positions_video_20230213.txt

QC News, May four, two thousand twenty-three: Representative Richie Yow was the only delegation member to respond in writing: I cannot speak on behalf of the entire delegation with specific answers to those questions. (auto-caption, corrected punctuation and proper nouns) Yow told QCN he never sought an Attorney General opinion and never told anyone he would. oct19_qcn_dualoffice_video_20230504.txtoct19_qcn_dualoffice_article_20230504.txt

The Attorney General's formal opinion

QC News, May four, two thousand twenty-three, quoting Assistant Attorney General Ellie Lister in a March twenty-two, two thousand twenty-three email to Senator Penry Gustafson: Therefore, it would violate the dual office provision of the South Carolina Constitution for an individual to serve in both positions And: I have discussed this issue with Solicitor General Cook and he agrees with my analysis. oct19_qcn_dualoffice_article_20230504.txt

The constitutional law analysis

QC News, Positions of Power video, February thirteen, two thousand twenty-three. University of South Carolina Constitutional Law Professor Scott Bauries: Carolina has a more aggressive form of it. You're just banned from holding dual offices, even if they don't conflict with each other. The idea behind it is to prevent corruption or probably also to prevent the appearance of corruption. (auto-caption, corrected punctuation and proper nouns) oct19_qcn_positions_video_20230213.txt

QC News, Positions of Power video. Professor Bauries: A school board member who assumes an appointed position with voting power on a technical college board, or vice versa — whatever office they took first, by law they lose it. They abdicate the office. But they still get to exercise the power of that office until legally they are declared not to be the holder of that power. (auto-caption, corrected punctuation and proper nouns) oct19_qcn_positions_video_20230213.txt

The courthouse

QC News, Positions of Power video, February thirteen, two thousand twenty-three. Barr narration, final line of the broadcast: If the delegation fails to find someone to replace Burch, there is another step to remove her from the college board. A taxpayer would have to go to the Chesterfield County courthouse and file a lawsuit asking a judge to rule on the dual office holding question. That lawsuit would be filed in the same courthouse where Judge Pau— The video ends mid-word. (auto-caption, corrected punctuation and proper nouns) oct19_qcn_positions_video_20230213.txt

The broadcast ends naming the courthouse. QC News reported one other option besides the delegation: a taxpayer suit asking a circuit court judge to remove her, filed at the Chesterfield County courthouse. Paul Burch has been a circuit court judge since nineteen ninety-one. The Governor's counsel wrote that her concurrent service would seemingly violate the prohibition; the Attorney General's office wrote on March twenty-two, two thousand twenty-three that it would violate it. As of QC News's May four, two thousand twenty-three report, the delegation had not set a meeting.

Adjacent to the record — not on the ballot: Judge Paul M. Burch

Judge Paul M. Burch is not on this ballot. He held House District Fifty-One before Kimberly Thomas Burch was elected to it, and he administered the school board’s oath of office; his House record, his co-sponsors and the joint election for his circuit seat are set out here for that reason, and for no other.

The minutes on disk break after March two thousand twenty-three and resume with the January two thousand twenty-five organizational meeting, where Burch was elected chair. The page already carries the January two thousand twenty-five election where she was chosen six to three over Coleman. She was a board member for the entire span the minutes cover before she held the chair.

The fiscal watch

QC News, March twelve, two thousand twenty-four: The South Carolina Department of Education has placed the Chesterfield County School District under a Fiscal Watch. And: The state Department of Education issued the notice after an audit this past December, which looked at the 2022–23 school year. oct19_qcn_fiscalwatch_20240312.txt

QC News, March twelve, two thousand twenty-four: Auditors say the district did not comply with wage rate requirements on federally funded construction contract language, did not record or reconcile certain purchasing card transactions, and did not properly document personnel expenses. oct19_qcn_fiscalwatch_20240312.txt

QC News, March twelve, two thousand twenty-four: According to the audit, the district did not timely claim certain federal funds and overclaimed funds, requiring the district to return $114,865 to the SC Department of Education. oct19_qcn_fiscalwatch_20240312.txt

QC News, March twelve, two thousand twenty-four, quoting the district statement: On February 23rd, the SC Department of Education placed Chesterfield County School District on a one-year fiscal watch designation as a result of the fiscal year 2023 Financial Statement Audit findings. oct19_qcn_fiscalwatch_20240312.txt

The audit covered the first year under Superintendent Chan Anderson. The findings included federally funded construction contract noncompliance, unreconciled purchasing card transactions, undocumented personnel expenses, and overclaimed federal funds requiring a return of one hundred fourteen thousand eight hundred sixty-five dollars. The board chair during that fiscal year was Chad L. Vick. The SCDE fiscal watch letter on this page is addressed to Vick. The designation lasted one year; the state removed the district from the fiscal watch in February two thousand twenty-five, during Burch's first year as chair.

The holdover provision

SC Code §59-53-510: commissioners of the Northeastern Technical College Area Commission serve for terms of three years and until their successors are appointed and qualify. oct18_sc_59_53_510.txt

The General Assembly honored Pete Owens of Chesterfield upon retirement from the NETC Area Commission after he served continuously for the past thirty years. oct18_s767_owens.txt

The statute creates the holdover by design. No sunset. No automatic vacancy. The term expires but the seat does not empty until a successor is appointed and qualifies. The Owens resolution proves the mechanism is not theoretical — it produced a thirty-year tenure on the same commission.

H. 5064, ratified and signed May fifteen, two thousand twenty-six as Act No. 156, sponsors Yow, Hayes, C. Mitchell, Luck and Williams, amends §59-53-510 to add three ex officio industry members — one per county, appointed by the legislative delegation. oct18_h5064_netc.txt

The act adds industry seats. It does not fix the holdover provision. The clause that says commissioners serve until their successors are appointed and qualify is unchanged by the amendment.

The bar credential

The ABA Journal, NOVEMBER 9, 2007: Judge Paul Burch's daughter, Kendall, is among the 20, although no formal appeal was filed on her behalf. oct17_aba_barexam.txt

Two phone calls preceded the decision. Twenty candidates were moved from fail to pass. The Board of Law Examiners chairman was not informed. The court characterized it as a scoring error. The chairman who made one of the calls was subsequently convicted of perjury and misconduct in office and sentenced to eighteen months. The bar credential Kendall Burch practices under exists because the Supreme Court eliminated the section after those calls.

The insulation layer

The South Carolina School Boards Association credentials board members through its Boardmanship Institute, publishes their profiles, trains their successors, lobbies the legislature for fiscal autonomy and against governance takeovers, and insures the district through the South Carolina School Boards Insurance Trust against the litigation its own conduct generates. When a case is filed against the district, SCSBIT absorbs the settlement. The settlement is confidential. The governance failures that produced the claim never reach the board. The board member whose conduct generated the claim is profiled as an exemplary leader. The next case starts from zero. The system that harms is the system that processes the harm, insures against it, and publishes the profile of the person who caused it.

The attorney who operates the separate Burch Law Firm served as Guardian ad Litem in the same circuit and subsequently served as closing attorney on the same property — first on the original mortgage, then on the sale. The firm's named partner, Spencer, serves as special referee for county tax seizures. The network that authored the legislation restructuring DSS's relationship with the people it serves holds the Guardian ad Litem appointments in the circuit where the same network adjudicates, prosecutes, and chairs the school board.

The oath

The oath and the office

Every person profiled on this page took an oath before assuming the authority their office carries.

›

Every person profiled on this page took an oath before assuming the authority their office carries. The oath is not a formality. It is the legal instrument that activates the power of the state in the hands of the individual. SC Constitution Article VI, Section Five prescribes the form; The words are: "I do solemnly swear or affirm that I am duly qualified, according to the Constitution of this State, to exercise the duties of the office to which I have been elected or appointed, and that I will, to the best of my ability, discharge the duties thereof, and preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution of this State and of the United States. So help me God." Without the oath, the person has no authority. With it, they carry the power to levy taxes, appropriate public funds, prosecute crimes, adjudicate disputes, administer elections, educate children, investigate deaths, and enforce the law. The offices these oaths activate were designed with separations. The council controls the budget but does not prosecute. The solicitor prosecutes but does not adjudicate. The judge adjudicates but does not enforce. The sheriff enforces but does not set the budget. The elections director administers the mechanism by which the public selects or replaces all of the above. The coroner investigates deaths independently of the sheriff because the statute recognizes that the person who enforces the law cannot also be the person who determines whether enforcement killed someone. Each separation exists because the framers understood that concentrating these functions produces the conditions the functions were designed to prevent. What this page documents is not that these officeholders violated their oaths in the way a criminal violates a statute. It documents that the separations the oaths were designed to protect have been dissolved through relationships the oaths do not address — law partnerships, shared congregations, overlapping employment, campaign endorsements, and professional networks that place every function of county governance within the reach of the same surnames. The oath says to the best of my ability, discharge the duties thereof. It does not say independently of your law partner or your former client. The network makes the distinction matter.

The page presents eight officeholders running without opposition on November third. The design of county governance separates their functions into branches. The grid on this page was built to show that separation. It is largely empty because the separation is largely formal. The judicial function has been held by Paul M. Burch since nineteen ninety-one. Roger Henderson sat alongside him for twenty-six years, first in Family Court and then in Circuit Court, after a decade as his law partner. Henderson chaired the Election Commission before he took the bench. He returned as a special prosecutor after he left it. The prosecutorial function passed to Paul Mike Burch Jr. in January of two thousand twenty-five. The education function is chaired by Kimberly Burch, whose board member Darin Coleman has held a seat for sixteen years while simultaneously employed at Northeastern Technical College. The former board chairman Chad Vick also transitioned to NETC employment. Two board officers are documented on NETC's payroll. The elections function is directed by Emory Henderson from the same office the retired judge chaired four decades earlier. The county council function is chaired by Mary Anderson, who simultaneously serves as SCAC president, McLeod Health board trustee, Lewis Realty broker-in-charge, and Project Hometown featured spokesperson. Seven of eleven county-level races on the November third ballot are unopposed. No campaign page exists for any of the eight unopposed incumbents profiled on this page. The columns on the grid exist. The lines between them run through the same surnames, the same law firms, the same professional networks, and the same podium.

What a council may do about a sheriff’s office

What a county council may and may not do about a sheriff’s office, in the statute, the Attorney General’s opinions and the state Supreme Court.

›

The statute: the county administrator shall exercise no authority over any elected officials of the county whose offices were created either by the Constitution or by the general law of the State. council_scstat_t04c009.txt

May 8, 1989, to Berkeley County: Consistent with these prior opinions, any action by the Berkeley County Council through its budgetary process cannot inter- fere with the Sheriff's role as chief law enforcement officer in his county. (a line break in the scan splits the word). law_scag_opinion_19890508_berkeley_sheriff.txt

August 17, 2020, to Jasper County: County Council has both the authority and the responsibility to make appropriations sufficient for the proper funding of the Sheriff's Department. In addition, consistent with prior opinions, this Office believes the County Council may not use its budgetary authority to interfere with the operating decisions of the Sheriff's Department. law_scag_opinion_20200817_jasper_sheriff.txt

If a court finds the Sheriff acted negligently in expending funds over the amount appropriated, he or she could be held personally liable. law_scag_opinion_20200817_jasper_sheriff.txt

March 29, 2024, to the Kershaw County sheriff: county councils do not have the authority through the budget process to interfere with the operations of a sheriff's department. We believe a court would likely determine county council members' limited authority over elected officials does not extend to giving direct orders to a county sheriff or his or her deputies during public county council meetings. law_scag_opinion_20240329_council_sheriff.txt

The Supreme Court, Decided April 27, 1992.: the threshold issue here is whether sheriffs and deputies are state officials. We hold they are. The case concerned liability for damages; it does not address a council's budget. law_cone_v_nettles_308sc109.txt

In short, as these opinions put it: the council must fund the sheriff’s office sufficiently and sets its appropriation; it may not use the budget to direct how the office operates.
